docs.t: Judge Marvin Aspen (N.D. Ill.) — Initial status and settlement
docs.x: Judge Marvin Aspen, N.D. Ill.. Initial status and settlement: Cases are set for status within 45 days of the complaint. The court strongly encourages consent to a magistrate judge.

docs.x: Judge Marvin Aspen, N.D. Ill.. docs.t: Judge Mary M. Rowland (N.D. Ill.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Mary M. Rowland, N.D. Ill.. Summary judgment (trap): Strict compliance with L.R. 56.1 is expected. File fact statements and responses separately from the memoranda, citing line, paragraph, or page, and make the evidence easy to find. Without leave, the movant is limited to 80 statements of undisputed material fact and the respondent to 40. In complex cases the court may request a timeline of events. Motions to strike are disfavored; raise objections to 56.1 material in the response or reply brief.

docs.t: Judge Mary M. Rowland (N.D. Ill.) — Discovery (trap)
docs.x: Judge Mary M. Rowland, N.D. Ill.. Discovery (trap): Discovery motions must fully comply with L.R. 37.2; an exchange of correspondence ordinarily does not suffice. At an impasse over voluminous electronically stored records, before moving to compel, the parties must meet in person with an IT representative of the system to be searched, and the requesting party should bring its own IT specialist.

docs.x: Judge Mary M. Rowland, N.D. Ill.. docs.t: Judge Mary M. Rowland (N.D. Ill.) — Initial status report
docs.x: Judge Mary M. Rowland, N.D. Ill.. Initial status report: The initial status hearing is usually about 60 days after filing. The report covers counsel, jurisdiction (citizenship of every member of an LLC, partnership, or association in diversity cases), claims, issues, unserved parties and service efforts, a deadline to amend or add parties, discovery dates, experts, trial readiness, unanimous magistrate-judge consent, and settlement status without offer details.

docs.t: Judge Mary M. Rowland (N.D. Ill.) — Emergency motions
docs.x: Judge Mary M. Rowland, N.D. Ill.. Emergency motions: Heard only in exceptional circumstances where delay would cause serious harm. Email the courtroom deputy with the case number in the subject line and a detailed message, copying counsel for all parties, and make reasonable efforts to give actual notice.

docs.t: Judge Mary M. Rowland (N.D. Ill.) — Criminal jury trials

docs.t: Judge Mary M. Rowland (N.D. Ill.) — Other practices
docs.x: Judge Mary M. Rowland, N.D. Ill.. Other practices: Judge Rowland allows more than one attorney per side to speak and encourages giving newer attorneys substantive speaking roles. Before submitting a settlement dismissal order, review Blue Cross & Blue Shield Ass’n v. American Express and Shapo v. Engle on retaining jurisdiction.

docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Discovery (trap)

docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Protective orders and sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. Motions in limine (trap): Due 14 days before the final pretrial conference; responses 7 days before; not bound with the pretrial order. docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Jury instructions and selection
docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. Jury instructions and selection: Use Seventh Circuit pattern instructions where they apply and Illinois Pattern Instructions for elements of Illinois claims. Agreed instructions are marked and numbered consecutively; disputed ones are numbered, name the proponent, and cite authority, with written objections citing authority. The judge uses a written juror questionnaire (samples are posted); propose only case-specific questions. The venire is about 24 people in civil cases and about 38 in single-defendant criminal cases; the court rules on cause challenges first, then peremptories alternate at sidebar, starting with plaintiff or the prosecution. Civil juries are typically twelve, all deliberating; criminal cases add one or two alternates.

docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. Trial: Trial days typically run 10 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. with about an hour for lunch. The final pretrial conference is about 1–2 weeks before trial; lead trial counsel with full authority must attend. Exhibits are shown on the courtroom’s evidence presentation system (jurors have individual screens), but keep a hard copy set ready for deliberations. Deliver a bench book of exhibits at or before trial unless excused. Learn the JERS system before the final pretrial conference. Request daily or expedited transcripts from the court reporter at least 7 days before trial.

docs.t: Judge Matthew Kennelly (N.D. Ill.) — Settlement conferences and warrants
docs.x: Judge Matthew Kennelly, N.D. Ill.. Settlement conferences and warrants: Plaintiff sends an itemized demand at least 14 days before the conference; defendant sends a written offer at least 7 days before. If unsettled, deliver copies to chambers (not filed) at least 2 days before. Parties with full authority (including insurers) must attend in person; phone availability is not acceptable except in the most extenuating circumstances. Under the judge’s standing order, search or seizure warrants in a criminal case assigned to the judge go to Judge Kennelly, not the duty, designated, or emergency magistrate judge.

docs.t: Judge Philip Godfrey Reinhard (N.D. Ill.) — Civil jury selection
docs.x: Judge Philip Godfrey Reinhard, N.D. Ill.. Civil jury selection: Submit an agreed case summary, a witness list with current addresses, and the names of everyone at counsel table. Normally 7 jurors are selected; each side gets 3 peremptories even with multiple parties. The court asks all voir dire questions. Challenges are made at sidebar juror by juror, alternating who goes first, and an accepted juror cannot be back-struck.

docs.t: Judge Philip Godfrey Reinhard (N.D. Ill.) — Trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Philip Godfrey Reinhard, N.D. Ill.. Trial (trap): Trial runs 9 a.m. to noon and 1:15 to 5 p.m., with one 15–20 minute recess each session. Tardiness is not tolerated, witnesses must fill the day, and trial continuances are rarely granted once a jury trial is set. Stand to address the court, question a witness, or object; state the precise ground without a speech. Ask permission the first time you approach a witness, otherwise stay at the podium, and do not greet adverse witnesses or use first names. Offer exhibits once foundation is laid and group exhibits with identical foundation. Arrange audio, video, or other equipment before trial, and advise the court in advance of any accommodation needs.

docs.x: Judge Philip Godfrey Reinhard, N.D. Ill.. Trial exhibits may not be used in opening statements without prior approval. Jury instructions must follow the Seventh Circuit criminal pattern instructions where applicable.

Before or with a default motion, file a declaration or chart giving, for each defendant and product, the 12 items listed in the standing order (units sold, sales dates, marketplaces, prices, sales volume, and restrained assets and the portion derived from the accused product), or explain in writing why an item cannot be provided.

docs.t: Judge Steven C. Seeger (N.D. Ill.) — Written discovery and discovery motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Steven C. Seeger, N.D. Ill.. Written discovery and discovery motions (trap): No boilerplate instructions or definitions in discovery requests; boilerplate objections without particularized reasons count for nothing. Discovery motions must state specifically when and how the movant complied with L.R. 37.2 (in person or by phone; emails or letters normally insufficient) or may be stricken. Be ready to argue at the hearing; a non-movant wanting to file a written response must ask at the outset. A motion to dismiss does not stay discovery, and there is no required order of discovery.

docs.x: Judge Steven C. Seeger, N.D. Ill.. Experts: Even non-report experts must be specifically designated, with a written statement of all Rule 702 opinions and their bases (Musser). Treating professionals need a report if their opinions go beyond their treatment and were formed because of the lawsuit. Daubert motions are due at least 60 days before trial unless ordered otherwise.

docs.x: Judge Steven C. Seeger, N.D. Ill.. docs.t: Judge Virginia Mary Kendall (N.D. Ill.) — Discovery

The judge presumptively requires a $10,000 bond per defendant. In utility patent cases, do not seek an asset restraint unless ABC Prods. (N.D. Ill. 2024) does not apply. docs.t: Judge Virginia Mary Kendall (N.D. Ill.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Virginia Mary Kendall, N.D. Ill.. Criminal matters: After arraignment, the schedule is: Rule 16.1 conference within 7 business days; pretrial motions 10 business days after that; responses 10 business days later; replies 7 business days later. The court strongly encourages in-person appearance at arraignments, detention hearings, pleas, and sentencings. If a change of plea will not go forward, tell the courtroom deputy at least one day ahead; deliver a draft plea agreement to Room 2506-A at least one day before the hearing. Two weeks before sentencing, the government must give the defense and the court a list of requested supervised-release conditions, each tied to support in the PSR, statute, record, or plea agreement, and file it; both sides initial the final marked-up list. Motions for early termination of supervised release must state the U.S. Attorney’s and probation officer’s

docs.t: Judge Virginia Mary Kendall (N.D. Ill.) — Settlement and appeals
docs.x: Judge Virginia Mary Kendall, N.D. Ill.. Settlement and appeals: For a settlement conference with the judge, plaintiff sends an itemized demand at least 14 days before, defendant responds in writing at least 7 days before, and both letters go to chambers no later than 2 days before (not filed). Parties with full settlement authority, including insurers, must attend in person; telephone availability is not acceptable except in the most extenuating circumstances. Bench-trial cases are usually referred to another judge or magistrate judge. Bankruptcy appeal briefs are due within 15 days of the bankruptcy court’s judgment, and extension motions must be filed in that period; briefs are limited to 15 pages. docs.t: Judge Ann D. Montgomery (D. Minn.) — Motion scheduling
docs.x: Judge Ann D. Montgomery, D. Minn.. Motion scheduling: Contact the calendar clerk (not the law clerks), who will give an oral argument date in almost all cases on request. You comply with the scheduling order’s dispositive motion deadline if you have filed the motion and received a hearing date from the calendar clerk before the deadline. Once a dispositive motion is set under the Local Rules, the judge will hear additional dispositive motions at the same time on a shorter schedule if counsel agree.

docs.x: Judge Ann D. Montgomery, D. Minn.. Special motions (trap): Motions to remand are briefed as dispositive motions; the judge decides whether to hear argument or refer to a magistrate judge. TRO, preliminary injunction, and Daubert motions are heard without witness testimony absent advance permission.

docs.t: Judge Ann D. Montgomery (D. Minn.) — Written submissions
docs.x: Judge Ann D. Montgomery, D. Minn.. Written submissions: Follow the Local Rules’ word limits. Additional briefing requires a written request in advance.

docs.t: Judge Ann D. Montgomery (D. Minn.) — Oral argument
docs.x: Judge Ann D. Montgomery, D. Minn.. Oral argument: Typically 15–20 minutes per side on dispositive motions, varying with the case and the day’s calendar; ask at the outset if unsure. docs.x: Judge Ann D. Montgomery, D. Minn.. Bifurcated argument for newer lawyers: The judge will consider split argument between a senior attorney and an associate who worked on the case, possibly with extra time. Ask the calendar clerk by phone or email at least one week before the hearing.

docs.t: Judge Ann D. Montgomery (D. Minn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Ann D. Montgomery, D. Minn.. Trial: Meet and confer before trial and jointly submit the agreed jury instructions. Mark exhibits before trial with plaintiff’s or defendant’s numbers and the case number. Examine from the lectern; approach the witness or jury only with permission; address witnesses and counsel by title, never first names; stand to object. Clerks or actors may read depositions when appropriate. Daily transcripts are not required but may be arranged with the court reporter. The judge may limit time for openings and closings.

docs.t: Judge Ann D. Montgomery (D. Minn.) — Settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Ann D. Montgomery, D. Minn.. Settlement conferences: All settlement conferences go to the magistrate judge, and every case set for trial will be noticed for one before trial. More than one is possible.

docs.t: Judge John R. Tunheim (D. Minn.) — Transcripts
docs.x: Judge John R. Tunheim, D. Minn.. Transcripts: Contact the court reporter, Kristine Mousseau, before any trial or hearing if requesting realtime or daily copy, with as much lead time as possible.

docs.t: Judge John R. Tunheim (D. Minn.) — Juror contact
docs.x: Judge John R. Tunheim, D. Minn.. Juror contact: Post-trial juror contact requires the judge’s written permission in all cases. If granted, contact is by letter only, not telephone, though jurors may call the attorneys in response.

docs.t: Judge John R. Tunheim (D. Minn.) — Settlement and chambers contact
docs.x: Judge John R. Tunheim, D. Minn.. Settlement and chambers contact: All settlement conferences go to the magistrate judge; request one any time through the magistrate judge. The judge may ask the magistrate judge to hold more. Contact the courtroom deputy, not the law clerks.

docs.t: Judge Katherine M. Menendez (D. Minn.) — Scheduling hearings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Katherine M. Menendez, D. Minn.. Scheduling hearings (trap): Schedule all motions through the courtroom deputy at 612-664-5140, saying when you expect to be ready to file. Tell the deputy about all pending or anticipated motions and any related motions in related cases, and alert the other side before you call. Hearings are usually set no sooner than two weeks after briefing closes, unless expedited. Even if the hearing is months out, you must file by the scheduling-order deadline and file all L.R. 7.1(b) or 7.1(c) documents at the same time. If the parties agree a motion can be decided on the papers, say so in the Notice of Hearing; the judge may still hold a hearing. To reschedule, have all counsel on the line at once.

docs.t: Judge Katherine M. Menendez (D. Minn.) — Contact with chambers
docs.x: Judge Katherine M. Menendez, D. Minn.. Contact with chambers: Chambers will not answer legal questions, including procedural questions governed by the FRCP, the Local Rules, or the scheduling order, and will not talk to the media. For a question about or clarification of an order, do not call; file a letter on CM/ECF. When calling about a case, identify yourself and your party and have the case name and number ready. CM/ECF filing questions go to the Clerk’s help desk at 612-664-5155.

docs.t: Judge Katherine M. Menendez (D. Minn.) — Courtesy copies and sealed filings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Katherine M. Menendez, D. Minn.. Courtesy copies and sealed filings (trap): No courtesy copies of motion papers, except for sealed filings the court cannot view on CM/ECF. Those must be hand-delivered to the Clerk’s Office, on paper or a data storage device, the same day they are filed. Sealed filings must follow Local Rule 5.6.

docs.t: Judge Katherine M. Menendez (D. Minn.) — Remote proceedings and status conferences
docs.x: Judge Katherine M. Menendez, D. Minn.. Remote proceedings and status conferences: Zoom requests go by email to menendez_chambers@mnd.uscourts.gov, copying opposing counsel. Agreement of both sides is ideal but not required, and the judge may order remote proceedings. The judge may set telephonic status conferences; for a conflict, call the deputy or email chambers to reschedule.

docs.t: Judge Katherine M. Menendez (D. Minn.) — Summary judgment and Daubert (trap)
docs.x: Judge Katherine M. Menendez, D. Minn.. Summary judgment and Daubert (trap): No summary judgment motion before the discovery deadline without leave, and no more than one summary judgment motion per party in a case without permission. Judge Menendez generally hears Daubert motions. One that would eliminate a claim or defense is filed with the dispositive motion and argued in the same memoranda, counting as one motion for the L.R. 7.1(f) word limit; one that only limits trial testimony is a motion in limine under the trial notice.

docs.t: Judge Katherine M. Menendez (D. Minn.) — TROs and expedited proceedings
docs.x: Judge Katherine M. Menendez, D. Minn.. TROs and expedited proceedings: Email a full set of papers to chambers the same day the motion is filed on ECF, serve the other side, and email contact information for both sides. The court then sets the hearing date and briefing schedule.

docs.t: Judge Katherine M. Menendez (D. Minn.) — Oral argument (trap)
docs.x: Judge Katherine M. Menendez, D. Minn.. Oral argument (trap): The judge reads the papers in advance and is likely to spend the hearing asking questions rather than hearing a prepared presentation. Email visual aids (e.g., PowerPoint) to the court and opposing counsel no later than the day before; no paper copies needed, and you may not get to present them. New case law or exhibits must go to opposing counsel first, with two copies for the court, but the judge prefers they be emailed to the court and counsel at least a day ahead. Newer lawyers who drafted or contributed significantly to the papers are strongly encouraged to argue; email ahead for accommodations such as divided time or consulting experienced counsel.

docs.t: Judge Katherine M. Menendez (D. Minn.) — Courtroom logistics
docs.x: Judge Katherine M. Menendez, D. Minn.. Courtroom logistics: Arrive early and double-check the location: the judge sits in Minneapolis but sometimes uses other courtrooms or courthouses. Address the court from the center podium into the microphone. Water is generally not provided except to witnesses and criminal defendants; lidded beverages are allowed. Learn the courtroom technology in advance and bring your own adapters; basic training can be arranged through the deputy. Have a back-up plan, since chambers is not responsible for the technology.

docs.t: Judge Laura Provinzino (D. Minn.) — Motion hearings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Laura Provinzino, D. Minn.. Motion hearings (trap): Do not call for a hearing date or file a Notice of Hearing with the motion. The court schedules hearings after filing, typically after the response; the courtroom deputy emails a suggested date, and the court issues the Notice of Hearing. If the parties agree a motion can be decided on the papers, they should file a Notice of Hearing saying so; the judge may still order a hearing. Contact the deputy at provinzino_chambers@mnd.uscourts.gov; the deputy answers questions about the judge’s practices but gives no legal advice.

docs.t: Judge Laura Provinzino (D. Minn.) — Meet and confer (trap)
docs.x: Judge Laura Provinzino, D. Minn.. Meet and confer (trap): The L.R. 7.1(a) meet-and-confer statement must state how the parties met (in person, video, telephone, or email), the date, and how long they discussed the motion.

docs.t: Judge Laura Provinzino (D. Minn.) — Motion types and Daubert
docs.x: Judge Laura Provinzino, D. Minn.. Motion types and Daubert: Motions to remand, transfer venue, and compel arbitration are briefed as dispositive motions, and Daubert and Markman motions are treated as dispositive. A Daubert motion that would eliminate a claim or defense is filed with the dispositive motion and argued in the same memoranda, counting as one motion for the L.R. 7.1(f) word limit. One that only limits trial testimony is a motion in limine.

docs.t: Judge Laura Provinzino (D. Minn.) — TROs and evidentiary hearings
docs.x: Judge Laura Provinzino, D. Minn.. TROs and evidentiary hearings: File the motion and papers, serve the other side, and email the deputy with contact information for all parties; the court then sets any hearing and briefing schedule. TROs, preliminary injunctions, and Daubert motions are typically heard without testimony. To present witnesses, notify the court and the other side and provide witness and exhibit lists as soon as possible, no later than three court days before the hearing.

docs.t: Judge Laura Provinzino (D. Minn.) — Early summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Laura Provinzino, D. Minn.. Early summary judgment (trap): Summary judgment before the close of discovery requires permission sought by a letter of no more than three pages stating the relief, whether fully or partially dispositive, whether the request is opposed, and why early consideration is warranted (specifying fact or expert discovery). The opponent may respond with a letter of no more than three pages within seven days. Denial is not a view on the merits.

docs.t: Judge Laura Provinzino (D. Minn.) — Briefs and exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Laura Provinzino, D. Minn.. Briefs and exhibits (trap): Motions to enlarge word limits are disfavored and must be filed at least three court days before the brief is due (L.R. 7.1(f)(1)(D)); do not file the longer brief until the request is granted. No courtesy copies unless requested. Digital media goes to the Clerk’s Office on a storage device. File each exhibit as a separate ECF attachment with a brief description, in searchable form where possible. Use full-page deposition transcripts, not compact (four-to-a-page) versions. Excerpts must include the cover page, the signature or verification page, and at least two pages before and after each excerpt.

docs.t: Judge Laura Provinzino (D. Minn.) — Supplemental authority
docs.x: Judge Laura Provinzino, D. Minn.. Supplemental authority: No advance permission needed. File a letter brief of no more than three pages explaining the authority’s relevance, with a copy of the authority; the opponent may respond with a letter of no more than three pages within seven days.

docs.t: Judge Laura Provinzino (D. Minn.) — Hearings and remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Laura Provinzino, D. Minn.. Hearings and remote appearances: Hearings are in person unless otherwise indicated, in Courtroom 3A at the St. Paul courthouse (check the location, which may vary). Remote hearings may be requested from the deputy but require good cause. Arrive at least 15 minutes early; hearings start on time. Stand at the lectern and observe formal decorum. For real-time or daily copy transcripts, email court reporter Lynne Krenz (lynne_krenz@mnd.uscourts.gov) before the trial or hearing, with as much lead time as possible.

docs.t: Judge Laura Provinzino (D. Minn.) — Oral argument (trap)
docs.x: Judge Laura Provinzino, D. Minn.. Oral argument (trap): Argument is a back-and-forth discussion, not a summary of the briefs; be ready for detailed questions about the record. There is no set time limit, but about 15 minutes per side is the benchmark. PowerPoint may not summarize or restate arguments or add new arguments or evidence; it may only highlight parts of the record. Email visual aids (other than filed exhibits) and any new legal authority to the court and opposing counsel at least one court day before the hearing. The judge prefers that the attorney who drafted or contributed significantly to the papers argue, and freely accommodates newer attorneys (divided time, bifurcated argument, consultation, or a few extra minutes for experienced counsel) on email request to the deputy.

docs.t: Judge Laura Provinzino (D. Minn.) — Trial and settlement
docs.x: Judge Laura Provinzino, D. Minn.. Trial and settlement: Be ready for trial by the magistrate judge’s trial readiness date, which is not a date certain. After summary judgment rulings, the deputy schedules a status conference to discuss trial dates, and a Trial Notice with deadlines follows; samples are at mnd.uscourts.gov/LMP. All settlement conferences go to the assigned magistrate judge, and more than one may be held.

docs.t: Judge Michael J. Davis (D. Minn.) — Contact with chambers
docs.x: Judge Michael J. Davis, D. Minn.. Contact with chambers: Contact the courtroom deputy at 612-664-5070, not the law clerks.

docs.t: Judge Michael J. Davis (D. Minn.) — Motion scheduling (trap)
docs.x: Judge Michael J. Davis, D. Minn.. Motion scheduling (trap): Follows the Local Rules for scheduling; all moving papers must be ready to file before you get a hearing date. Civil motions are typically heard Thursdays, with multiple hearings set for the same time; the judge sets the order just before the hearing, so check in with the courtroom deputy. Parties with several motions that day should agree on their order in advance. Dispositive motions are argued at least 42 days after the motion papers are filed, and often later. Dispositive motions are occasionally referred to the magistrate judge, case by case. No summary judgment motion before the discovery deadline without special permission from the court. File motions or stipulations to extend deadlines well in advance, leaving the court time to review the fully briefed motion before the hearing.

docs.t: Judge Michael J. Davis (D. Minn.) — TROs and Daubert
docs.x: Judge Michael J. Davis, D. Minn.. TROs and Daubert: For expedited matters such as a TRO, submit two sets of courtesy copies the same day the motion is e-filed, serve the other side, and give chambers contact information for both sides; the court then sets the hearing date and briefing schedule. Judge Davis hears Daubert motions personally. Call the courtroom deputy to schedule one after expert reports are filed but well before the motion in limine deadline. TRO, preliminary injunction, and Daubert motions are heard without witness testimony absent advance permission.

docs.t: Judge Michael J. Davis (D. Minn.) — Written submissions and courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Michael J. Davis, D. Minn.. Written submissions and courtesy copies (trap): Follow the Local Rules’ word and page limits. Do not file a separate motion for each count to gain briefing space. Extensions are disfavored and require an advance written request. Send two courtesy copies of motion papers, organized, tabbed as appropriate, three-hole punched, and bound, stapled, or clamped; filings over 1.5 inches must be tabbed in a binder. Do not wrap sealed copies separately; put them in the proper binders. Pay particular attention to the Local Rules and ECF rules on sealed and redacted filings.

docs.t: Judge Michael J. Davis (D. Minn.) — Oral argument
docs.x: Judge Michael J. Davis, D. Minn.. Oral argument: Generally no more than 15 minutes per side on dispositive motions. Arrive at least 15 minutes early to check in; stand at the podium and be formal. The judge reads the briefs in advance, so don’t repeat the facts. New case law offered at argument must first go to opposing counsel, with 2 copies for the court. Use the courtroom technology; the courtroom deputy can arrange training.

docs.t: Judge Michael J. Davis (D. Minn.) — Newer lawyers
docs.x: Judge Michael J. Davis, D. Minn.. Newer lawyers: Judge Davis encourages newer lawyers to argue motions and examine witnesses at trial, and will allow bifurcated argument to give them the chance. Contact chambers with questions.

docs.t: Judge Michael J. Davis (D. Minn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Michael J. Davis, D. Minn.. Trial: Meet and confer before trial and jointly submit the agreed jury instructions; stipulate to as many exhibits as possible. Attorney voir dire is by request; if granted, generally 10–15 minutes per side. Videotaped depositions must be edited down to the heart of the matter, or their use will be curtailed. Trial days generally run 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., with two 15-minute breaks and an hour for lunch; have enough witnesses to fill each day until 5:00 p.m. Stand and use the counsel-table microphones for objections; examine from the lectern; no permission needed to approach a witness. Provide a clean exhibit list for the jury before deliberations listing only admitted exhibits, reviewed by both sides and the court. Post-trial juror contact requires the judge’s written permission in all cases.

docs.t: Judge Michael J. Davis (D. Minn.) — Settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Michael J. Davis, D. Minn.. Settlement conferences: All settlement conferences go to the magistrate judge (complicated cases may also go to a special master). Request one any time through the magistrate judge; the court often orders additional conferences before trial.

docs.t: Judge Nancy E. Brasel (D. Minn.) — Motion scheduling (trap)

One that only limits trial testimony is brought as a motion in limine under the trial notice, which issues after the final ruling on dispositive motions and a final settlement conference.

docs.t: Judge Nancy E. Brasel (D. Minn.) — Oral argument
docs.x: Judge Nancy E. Brasel, D. Minn.. Oral argument: Arrive at least 15 minutes early. Stand at the podium and address the court and counsel with civility and formality. docs.t: Judge Nancy E. Brasel (D. Minn.) — Motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Nancy E. Brasel, D. Minn.. Motions in limine (trap): No more than five motions in limine without extraordinary circumstances and prior permission, each on one discrete issue. Video recordings must be pre-edited, with disputes raised by motion in limine. Contacting jurors after trial requires Judge Brasel’s written permission in all cases.

docs.t: Judge Nancy E. Brasel (D. Minn.) — Settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Nancy E. Brasel, D. Minn.. Settlement conferences: All settlement conferences go to the magistrate judge, and more than one may be held.

A Daubert motion that would knock out a claim or defense must be brought with the dispositive motion and argued in the same memoranda, and the two count as one motion for the Local Rule 7.1(f) word limit. Multiple summary judgment motions filed at about the same time count as one for word limits (Local Rule 7.1(c)(4)). docs.t: Judge Patrick J. Schiltz (D. Minn.) — Oral argument (trap)
docs.x: Judge Patrick J. Schiltz, D. Minn.. Oral argument (trap): No time limits; argument continues until the judge’s questions are answered and counsel’s points are made. The judge reads the briefs and uses argument for back-and-forth, so be ready for detailed questions, including about the record. PowerPoint may not be used to summarize or restate arguments or add new arguments or evidence, only to highlight particular parts of the record. Meet and confer and jointly file one set of proposed jury instructions, each citing current supporting authority. docs.t: Judge Patrick J. Schiltz (D. Minn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Patrick J. Schiltz, D. Minn.. Trial: A trial notice with detailed instructions issues about 90 days before a civil trial. Pretrial conferences are typically Fridays and trials start Mondays. The judge conducts voir dire. Trial days generally run 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with two 15-minute breaks and lunch from 12:00 to 1:30 p.m. Have witnesses to fill each day, and give 24 hours’ notice of each day’s witnesses. Mark exhibits per the trial notice and have paper copies to show witnesses before admission; admitted exhibits may be published electronically. docs.x: Judge Paul A. Magnuson, D. Minn.. Daubert motions: Judge Magnuson, not the magistrate judge, typically hears Daubert motions. Call the deputy to schedule after expert reports are served but well before the motion in limine deadline.

docs.t: Judge Susan Richard Nelson (D. Minn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Susan Richard Nelson, D. Minn.. Trial: A trial notice with detailed instructions issues at least two months before trial. Mark exhibits to match the exhibit list and deliver two sets of hard copies to chambers in binders tabbed by exhibit number before trial. Submit a joint statement of the case to read during voir dire. The judge conducts most of voir dire; counsel usually get 10–15 minutes afterward. Edit videotaped depositions and raise disputes in limine. Have enough witnesses to take testimony every day until 5:00 p.m.

docs.t: Judge Susan Richard Nelson (D. Minn.) — Settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Susan Richard Nelson, D. Minn.. Settlement conferences: Most settlement conferences go to the magistrate judge; request one any time. More than one is allowed.

docs.t: Judge M. Hannah Lauck (E.D. Va.) — Hearings on civil motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge M. Hannah Lauck, E.D. Va.. Hearings on civil motions (trap): Local Civil Rule 7(E) does not apply in civil cases assigned to Chief Judge Lauck. No motion is deemed withdrawn just because no party requested a hearing or filed a formal waiver of hearing. The court schedules a hearing only if it decides one is necessary after reviewing the briefs.

docs.t: Judge M. Hannah Lauck (E.D. Va.) — Generative AI disclosure (trap)
docs.x: Judge M. Hannah Lauck, E.D. Va.. Generative AI disclosure (trap): Any party that uses generative artificial intelligence to prepare a filing must identify that use in the filing and certify that it has reviewed all citations for accuracy.

docs.t: Judge Roderick C. Young (E.D. Va.) — Hearings on civil motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Roderick C. Young, E.D. Va.. Hearings on civil motions (trap): Local Civil Rule 7(E) does not apply in civil cases assigned to Judge Young. No motion is deemed withdrawn just because no party requested a hearing or filed a formal waiver of hearing. The court schedules a hearing only if it decides one is necessary after reviewing the briefs.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Ray (S.D. Ga.) — Motions court; no informal requests (trap)
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Ray, S.D. Ga.. Motions court; no informal requests (trap): Magistrate Judge Ray will not consider informal requests to the courtroom deputy or chambers for rulings on any issue, including extensions of time. Any ruling of any kind requires a motion on the docket. Letter briefs are not accepted except under the informal discovery conference and settlement conference procedures. Inquiries go to courtroom deputy Molly Davenport (molly_davenport@gas.uscourts.gov, 912-650-4035).

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Ray (S.D. Ga.) — Discovery disputes: conference first (trap)
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Ray, S.D. Ga.. Discovery disputes: conference first (trap): No discovery motion may be filed without the court’s permission after an informal discovery dispute video conference. This covers Rule 37 motions, Rule 26 protective-order motions, and Rule 45 motions to quash or compel when compliance is in this District, but not Rule 26(a)(1)(B)-exempt proceedings, cases with an unrepresented party, or Daubert motions and motions to strike experts (though the court may apply it to any dispute on notice). File the Motion for an Informal Discovery Dispute Conference on ECF (Civil – Motions – Motion for Informal Discovery Dispute Conference) using the court’s form, giving at least three mutually agreeable dates and times within two weeks of filing. Before asking, counsel must meet and confer under LR 26.5, which the court expects to mean actually speaking with each other (in

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Ray (S.D. Ga.) — Discovery letter briefs (trap)
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Ray, S.D. Ga.. Discovery letter briefs (trap): At least 24 hours before the conference, each side emails the courtroom deputy a letter brief addressed to Judge Ray (not filed on the docket), served on all counsel: no more than three pages single-spaced plus up to ten pages of exhibits, factual and non-argumentative, naming who will appear. Only disputes in the letters are considered, and be ready to raise all pending discovery issues: failing to raise an existing dispute may be treated as a waiver.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Ray (S.D. Ga.) — After the discovery conference
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Ray, S.D. Ga.. After the discovery conference: The conference is not on the record; the court may not issue a written ruling and may just note the conference in a text entry. If the dispute is not resolved, the parties have ten days to file a discovery motion.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Ray (S.D. Ga.) — Settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Ray, S.D. Ga.. Settlement conferences: On consent, parties may move for a settlement conference with Judge Ray, offering at least four mutually agreeable dates no later than 2 months after filing. The case must be ready for meaningful settlement discussions. All parties, including at least one person with full settlement authority, must attend in person with counsel; remote attendance only for good cause (the worksheet says a substantial showing, and mere convenience is not enough). At least one week before, jointly email the Settlement Conference Worksheet to the courtroom deputy (do not file it). Written settlement statements are not required unless the court gives at least 48 hours’ notice, and then follow the letter-brief length limits.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Ray (S.D. Ga.) — Search warrant applications
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Ray, S.D. Ga.. Search warrant applications: Search warrant applications are heard each business day at 2:00 p.m.; agents and the U.S. Attorney’s Office must submit all papers by 4:30 p.m. the preceding business day, absent truly extraordinary circumstances. Email each application to the courtroom deputy as one text-searchable PDF with the application, supporting documents, and affidavits in the order the AUSA expects to discuss them. Changes after the 4:30 p.m. deadline may delay processing; emergency requests need a showing of need by email or phone first.

docs.t: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl (D. Wyo.) — Case management plan
docs.x: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl, D. Wyo.. Case management plan: The Joint Case Management Plan form asks for, among other things, the Rule 26(f) attendees, parties and parent entities (for recusal), related cases, a nature-of-the-case statement of 2 pages or less, and a jurisdiction statement; in diversity cases, state every party’s citizenship, including each partner or member of a partnership or LLC. Propose expert disclosure, fact discovery, and trial dates on the expectation that trial occurs within approximately nine months of the Initial Pretrial Conference, absent unusual circumstances. The plan is subject to revision at the conference.

docs.t: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl (D. Wyo.) — Exhibits and the final pretrial order (trap)
docs.x: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl, D. Wyo.. Exhibits and the final pretrial order (trap): Exhibit lists in the final pretrial order sort objections into Category A (admissible without further proof), B (objections other than foundation, such as hearsay or relevance), and C (foundation, identification, or authenticity only). Failing to mark a foundation objection waives it, and a party that proves foundation over objection may move for fees and costs. Before trial, give the court one hard copy (tabbed ringed binder with the exhibit list in front) and one electronic copy of all exhibits. Provide electronic trial exhibits for JERS on a USB drive, DVD, or CD to the Clerk’s Office at least 7 days before trial (PDF/JPG/BMP/TIF/GIF; AVI/WMV/MPG/MP3/MP4/WMA/WAV; files no larger than 500MB). Five business days before trial, email the court reporter (megan_strawn@wyd.uscourts.gov) exhibit and witness lists

docs.t: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl (D. Wyo.) — Depositions at trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl, D. Wyo.. Depositions at trial (trap): Notify opposing counsel of deposition offers at least 10 business days before trial; objections or counter-designations are due at least 5 business days before trial, and unresolved differences go to the court in writing at least 3 business days before trial.

docs.t: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl (D. Wyo.) — Witnesses
docs.x: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl, D. Wyo.. Witnesses: Listing a “will call” witness guarantees the witness’s presence at trial. In jury cases, give the court an estimate of each witness’s time on the stand at least 7 days before trial, and tell opposing counsel during trial which witnesses you will call the next day.

docs.t: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl (D. Wyo.) — Jury instructions and voir dire (trap)
docs.x: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl, D. Wyo.. Jury instructions and voir dire (trap): Proposed voir dire, jury instructions, and verdict forms are due 7 days before trial. The court provides stock instructions; submit substantive instructions (and any requested changes to stock ones) in three sets with citations: Set A agreed, Set B plaintiff’s disputed, Set C defendant’s disputed. File them and also email them to chambers (wyojudgesws@wyd.uscourts.gov) in Word or WordPerfect. At the same time, file a brief, noncontentious joint statement of the case (“Plaintiff contends . . . ; Defendant contends . . .” where the parties can’t agree).

docs.t: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl (D. Wyo.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl, D. Wyo.. Jury selection: Fourteen jurors are seated for voir dire; after the panel is passed for cause, each side exercises up to three peremptory challenges in writing, alternating starting with plaintiff, and the first eight unchallenged jurors are the jury. Each side gets thirty minutes of its own voir dire after the court’s. Jury trials start at 9:00 a.m. in Casper.

docs.t: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl (D. Wyo.) — Bench trials: findings and conclusions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl, D. Wyo.. Bench trials: findings and conclusions (trap): Plaintiff submits proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law at least ten days before trial and defendant five days before trial; file them and email them to chambers in Word or WordPerfect. Plaintiff’s facts go in simple declarative sentences in numbered paragraphs, with no recitation of testimony or admissions, no pejoratives or legal conclusions, so each sentence can be admitted or denied; legal contentions go in numbered paragraphs, each followed by authority. Defendant’s response admits or denies each sentence using plaintiff’s numbering, then adds its own affirmative facts and responsive legal contentions in the same format.

docs.t: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl (D. Wyo.) — Bench trials: written direct testimony (trap)
docs.x: Judge Scott W. Skavdahl, D. Wyo.. Bench trials: written direct testimony (trap): Expert witnesses and witnesses on significant technical matters give direct testimony by an unsworn narrative written statement (not Q&A), which the witness adopts under oath at trial and the party offers as an exhibit; live supplementation is limited and expected to be minimal. Not for adverse parties or subpoenaed witnesses. Exhibits are not attached to the statements but pre-marked and exchanged as usual. The expert procedure requires exchange and filing no later than 14 days before trial (or as the initial pretrial order sets); the bench-trial pretrial form says 7 days before the final pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Contacts and emergencies
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Contacts and emergencies: Routine matters go to the case management team; case-specific matters go by email to the law clerk assigned by the case number’s last digit (1–3 Ethan Wang, 4–6 William Bock IV, 7–9 Vance Kelley; for 0, use the last nonzero digit). For an emergency motion needing a hearing on the record, call chambers and follow up by email to Divine_Chambers@moed.uscourts.gov. For same-day relief, call the assigned clerk.

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Briefs: limits and format (trap)
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Briefs: limits and format (trap): Memoranda supporting or opposing a motion are limited to 15 pages and replies to 8 pages, with one-inch margins, double spacing (except footnotes), and 11-point Century Schoolbook throughout. Anything over 10 pages needs a table of contents and table of authorities, with asterisks in the left margin marking the chief authorities. Start the heading of any motion needing consent (such as an extension) with “Opposed,” “Unopposed,” or a variation, and end it with a certificate of conference giving the date, time, manner, and participants (not needed for dispositive or injunction motions). Motions lacking a required certificate may be stricken. Failing to oppose a motion or respond to an argument may be treated as a concession. Proposed orders are filed as a PDF attachment and emailed to the assigned clerk in word-processing forma

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Pleadings: one-document rule (trap)
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Pleadings: one-document rule (trap): After filing a complaint, counterclaim, or crossclaim, send opposing counsel a .doc or .docx copy. Answers must be prepared in that Word document, with each response in a non-numbered paragraph directly below the allegation (not for pro se parties or appeals). Amended pleadings must include a redline against the original as the final attachment. A party opposing a motion to dismiss must say whether amendment can cure the problem; otherwise the court is disinclined to allow a later amendment.

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Extensions and case management order (trap)
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Extensions and case management order (trap): Extensions are strongly discouraged; a first extension over three weeks, or any later extension, requires exceptional or compelling circumstances. Joint stipulations to extend or reschedule are not honored; file a motion at least four business days before the first affected date stating the current date, time requested, grounds, prior extensions, effect on other deadlines, and a proposed schedule after conferring. Case management order changes outside Rule 29 need a motion with an updated draft order at least four business days before the deadline and exceptional circumstances, which do not include press of business, slow discovery, or delay in starting discovery. Expect trial in the order’s window.

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Multiple parties and summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Multiple parties and summary judgment (trap): Co-parties must file joint motions and joint memoranda on the same or similar issues, under the same page limits. Each movant may file only one summary judgment motion and one Rule 702/703 motion covering all experts. Multiple movants file one consolidated statement of material facts and respondents one consolidated response. Send the statement to opponents in .doc/.docx; the response is written in that document, with each disputed fact explained in a non-numbered paragraph below it. Unanswered facts are deemed admitted; additional facts go in a separate, numbered filing. A joint statement of uncontested facts is due within 10 days after summary judgment briefing is complete. The court prefers dispositive motions fully briefed 120 days before trial.

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Discovery disputes (trap): No discovery motion without the court’s approval. After meeting and conferring (letters, emails, or texts don’t count), email the assigned clerk to request a telephone conference, with a certificate of conference. The same applies to disputes with nonparties, who must be told of these procedures; incarcerated pro se cases may confer in writing and file without approval. After the conference is scheduled, the movant files a one- to two-page single-spaced motion and the opponent a one- to two-page response within three business days, raising no new issues; include the disputed request and objection. Motions to compel are due no more than 11 days after the discovery deadline. Boilerplate and general objections (including “to the extent that” preambles) will be disregarded or stricken; object specifically to each request. Use Rule 29 st

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Sealing, protective orders, and filing
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Sealing, protective orders, and filing: Email proposed protective orders to the assigned clerk; any that mention sealing must require the parties to ask the court to remove sealed documents within thirty days after the case ends, or they will be unsealed. The court strongly prefers redaction to sealing. Filings must be text-searchable PDFs converted directly from word processing; OCR any scanned exhibits. Edit exhibits to the pertinent parts and highlight them. No courtesy copies except a courtesy copy of exhibits brought to trial.

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Generative AI certificate (trap)
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Generative AI certificate (trap): Every attorney and pro se litigant must file, with the notice of appearance, an “AI notice” (CM/ECF Notices) certifying that no filing will be drafted by generative AI or that any AI-drafted language will be fully checked by a human using print reporters or traditional legal databases. Sanctions for fake or misrepresented cases can include fines, striking, and dismissal.

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Rule 16, ADR, and settlement
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Rule 16, ADR, and settlement: The court sets a Rule 16 conference after all defendants answer. The parties submit one joint plan, signed by all, on the judge’s Case Management Order template, with disputes in an appendix; plaintiff initiates. Track ranges: expedited (disposition within 12 months, 120 days of discovery), standard (18 months, 180–240 days), complex (24 months, 240–360 days). Lead trial counsel must attend. Civil cases (except habeas, Social Security, and bankruptcy appeals) are referred to ADR; plaintiff’s counsel is lead counsel unless the parties agree otherwise. A neutral not on the certified list needs a motion and special expertise. ADR extensions need a motion at least four business days before the deadline. On settlement, notify the court immediately; dismissal papers are due within 30 days.

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Pretrial filings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Pretrial filings (trap): Civil trials sit on a three-week docket; be ready on day one and on twenty-four hours’ notice. By 10 days before trial: joint stipulation of uncontested facts, one-page joint case summary, motions in limine (all in one document per party; responses in 7 days), exhibit and witness lists, exhibits delivered to the clerk, deposition and discovery designations, and objections to demonstratives (which are listed 14 days and exchanged 10 days before trial). Plaintiff numbers exhibits from 1 and defendants from 1000; the list must flag business records to be authenticated under FRE 902(11) or (12). Exhibit and designation objections are due 7 days before trial or may be waived. Voir dire questions, 404(b) notices, and unresolved recording-transcript disputes are due 7 days before trial. Jury instructions: exchange 14 days out, meet and confe

docs.t: Judge Josh Divine (E.D. Mo.) — Trial conduct (trap)
docs.x: Judge Josh Divine, E.D. Mo.. Trial conduct (trap): The court conducts voir dire; counsel may get up to 20 minutes after. Openings and closings are limited to 20 minutes per side. Raise preliminary matters 15 minutes before the trial day, at lunch, or at day’s end, never when the jury is ready. Objections are a word or phrase with no argument before the jury; ask for a further record at the next recess. No re-cross unless new matter arises on redirect, do not call a witness an “expert,” and don’t talk with your witness between tender for cross and redirect. Send next-day witness lists by 7:00 p.m. Stand when speaking. Only attorneys may use devices without approval (silenced); non-attorneys power off. Schedule ELMO training before trial (not on trial day) and bring your own audio player.

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Hearings and appearances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Hearings and appearances (trap): Civil law and motion on designated Thursdays at 1:30 p.m.; criminal law and motion on Thursdays at 9:00 a.m.; Courtroom 7, 14th floor, Sacramento. Dates are not reserved, but get available dates by emailing the courtroom deputy, Gabriel Michel (gmichel@caed.uscourts.gov). Bail-review motions are not noticed on the criminal calendar. Oral argument on all motions is in person. In civil cases, joint requests to appear remotely must be made at least one week before the hearing and are generally disfavored. Civil papers must say whether the party wants the motion decided without oral argument; the court may take any motion under submission under Local Rule 230(g) and will say so by minute order before the hearing. Criminal motions must say whether an evidentiary hearing is requested and how long it would take; be ready to ar

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Briefing and page limits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Briefing and page limits (trap): Civil and criminal: 12-point font, footnotes no more than two sizes smaller, and a sans serif font such as Arial or Helvetica encouraged. Moving and opposition briefs are capped at 25 pages and replies at 15 without prior leave, granted only for good cause; pages over the limit will not be considered. No supplemental briefs or sur-replies without prior leave. Paginate multi-page exhibits internally starting at 1 and cite them by exhibit and page (e.g., Ex. A at 7).

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Civil meet and confer (trap)
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Civil meet and confer (trap): In represented civil cases, counsel must meet and confer before filing any motion to discuss its substance and possible resolution, settling minor procedural matters along the way. The notice of motion must certify that meet-and-confer efforts were exhausted, with a very brief summary; noncompliant motions are summarily denied without prejudice.

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Summary judgment and cross-motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Summary judgment and cross-motions (trap): Read Local Rule 260. Before filing, meet and confer on stipulated facts and file them as a Joint Statement of Undisputed Facts, plus a Separate Statement for facts not stipulated. The nonmovant reproduces and responds and may file a concise Statement of Disputed Facts; the movant responds to that but may not reply to the nonmovant’s response. At least 28 days before the dispositive-motion deadline, meet and confer about cross-motions. If cross-motions are planned, only four briefs are allowed: plaintiff’s opening (25 pages) at least 14 days before the deadline, noticed for hearing at least 42 days out; defendant’s opposition and cross-motion (35 pages) 14 days later; plaintiff’s reply and opposition (20 pages) 14 days later; and defendant’s reply (10 pages) 10 days later. The four-brief limit applies even with

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Proposed orders and ex parte applications
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Proposed orders and ex parte applications: Proposed orders are not required with civil motions except for TROs and preliminary injunctions; also submit proposed consent decrees where applicable and proposed findings and conclusions after a bench trial. Any required proposed order must follow Local Rule 137(b) and be emailed in Word to DJCorders@caed.uscourts.gov. Ex parte applications are usually decided on the papers. Before filing, contact the courtroom deputy and the opposing party; the papers must say whether an opposition will be filed and include an affidavit explaining the need for the order, why a stipulation could not be obtained, and why the matter cannot be noticed under Local Rule 230.

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Sealing and protective orders (trap)
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Sealing and protective orders (trap): Nothing is sealed or filed redacted without prior court approval (except Local Rule 140 redactions). Sealing or redaction requests about the record on a motion Judge Calabretta will decide go to Judge Calabretta, not the magistrate judge. The request must say whether it is opposed; if it is opposed or silent, other parties must file an opposition or non-opposition within three days of service. File the Notice of Request electronically, and email the request, a proposed order in Word, and the documents to DJCorders@caed.uscourts.gov; once the order is entered, email the documents to ApprovedSealed@caed.uscourts.gov. Discovery protective orders do not govern sealing on the public docket, and only the proponent of sealing may request it. Give the designating party enough advance notice to seek sealing before you file

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Extensions and continuances
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Extensions and continuances: Stipulations extending deadlines or modifying rules have no effect until approved. File well in advance, listing the existing date and all other set dates (discovery cutoff, last motion hearing date, pretrial conference, and trial), specific good-cause reasons, and any prior requests and their outcome. In civil cases, saying an extension “will promote settlement” is not enough; describe the status of negotiations with specificity. Stipulations continuing dispositive-motion dates (civil) or the trial date are disfavored.

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Initial case management (civil)
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Initial case management (civil): Plaintiff must complete service within 90 days of filing and serve the new-case orders on all parties (the removing party does so in removed cases), filing a certificate of service. Rule 7.1 disclosure statements are due on first appearance. Within 60 days of service of the complaint on any party, or of removal, the parties must confer under Rule 26(f) and file a joint status report covering the listed topics (a) through (p), including proposed dates for the last motion hearing, final pretrial conference, and trial, Rule 702 limits, and settlement timing, VDRP position, and whether the trial judge may act as settlement judge. The report must say whether the parties want a status conference or are content with a scheduling order on the papers; significant disagreements should be expected to draw a status conference.

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Civil pretrial
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Civil pretrial: File a Joint Pretrial Statement under Local Rule 281 seven days before the Final Pretrial Conference and email it in Word to DJCorders@caed.uscourts.gov. Separate statements are allowed only for unrepresented parties. It must include a neutral joint statement of the case, a separate joint exhibit list (JX-1, JX-2) for overlapping exhibits, plaintiff’s exhibits by number and defendant’s by letter, detailed exhibit descriptions (date, Bates number, description, page length), every remaining issue under points of law or marked abandoned, anticipated motions in limine, and trial length. Do not file motions in limine before the pretrial conference; the pretrial order sets those and other trial deadlines.

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Jury trials
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Jury trials: Civil: 8 jurors and no alternates (deviations by motion); 16 in the box; typically 20 minutes of attorney voir dire per side after the court’s questioning; 3 peremptories each, exercised by strike-or-pass with no waiver by passing, but once one side is out of strikes the other may use only two more. Criminal: 12 jurors, typically 2 alternates; 22 in the box; typically 20 minutes of attorney voir dire per side; peremptories per Fed. R. Crim. P. 24(b) and (c)(4); after 6 are removed the court refills the front row. Jury instructions are filed jointly as a single set after the Final Pretrial Conference (civil) or Trial Confirmation Hearing (criminal), with objections and any alternate noted with the contested instruction. Do not include the listed Ninth Circuit preliminary instructions the court gives after voir dire unless seeking a modified

docs.t: Judge Daniel Calabretta (E.D. Cal.) — Criminal motions, plea, and sentencing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Daniel Calabretta, E.D. Cal.. Criminal motions, plea, and sentencing (trap): Local Rule 302(b)(1) motions go to Judge Calabretta; other pretrial motions go to the magistrate judge. File at least 14 days before the hearing; oppose (or file a non-opposition) within 7 days; reply within 4 days after the opposition is due. A party that did not timely oppose will not be heard at argument. All pretrial motions except motions in limine must be heard at least 30 days before the Trial Confirmation Hearing, where the court sets in-limine, exhibit, and other trial deadlines. Rule 16 requests and disclosures should be made before trial dates are set. Open pleas: the government files elements, maximum penalties, and a proposed factual basis 5 days before the change of plea, and the defense files any alternative 2 days before. The government must give notice if it will seek remand of an out-of-c

docs.t: Judge Paul L. Maloney (W.D. Mich.) — Courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Paul L. Maloney, W.D. Mich.. Courtesy copies (trap): Submit a courtesy copy of all dispositive motions, responses, and replies, with all exhibits, directly to chambers within 24 hours of filing, by hand delivery or first-class mail. It must comply with W.D. Mich. LCivR 7.2(b)(iii)/LCrR 47.1(b)(iii). Print courtesy copies from the docket so they show the ECF header and PageID numbers, and bind them (any binding that keeps pages together). Unpublished opinions attached to the original need not be included. Chambers: 410 W. Michigan Ave., Kalamazoo, MI 49007; (269) 381-4741.

docs.t: Judge Paul L. Maloney (W.D. Mich.) — Courtroom technology
docs.x: Judge Paul L. Maloney, W.D. Mich.. Courtroom technology: The Kalamazoo courtroom has a large projection screen plus monitors at the witness stand, lectern, counsel tables, and bench; the witness and lectern monitors allow annotation. The court strongly encourages using the equipment. Arrange training and practice well in advance through courttech@miwd.uscourts.gov; testing must happen before the day of the proceeding, as the courtroom and staff are not available for it that day.

docs.t: Judge Algenon L. Marbley (S.D. Ohio) — Oral argument by newer attorneys
docs.x: Judge Algenon L. Marbley, S.D. Ohio. Oral argument by newer attorneys: In civil cases, after a motion is fully briefed, any party may file a Notice requesting oral argument and representing that a newer attorney (out of law school 6 years or less) will argue all or part of it. No opposition briefing is entertained. The court grants the request if practicable and sets argument on an expedited basis; experienced counsel may assist. No inference is drawn from not using a newer attorney, and the judge encourages newer attorneys’ participation in all proceedings.

docs.t: Judge Algenon L. Marbley (S.D. Ohio) — Civil trial setting and continuances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Algenon L. Marbley, S.D. Ohio. Civil trial setting and continuances (trap): The court uses a trailing docket of 3 to 5 civil cases set for the same day, tried in filing order; if an earlier case goes to trial, the next case must stay ready on standby for 2 weeks unless ordered otherwise. Criminal matters get preference. The trial date will be continued only on a written motion with an affidavit showing exceptional circumstances, made immediately upon learning of them. Trials run Monday through Thursday, 9 a.m. to about 5 p.m.; Fridays are reserved for final pretrials, criminal matters, and motion hearings.

docs.t: Judge Algenon L. Marbley (S.D. Ohio) — Settlement conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Algenon L. Marbley, S.D. Ohio. Settlement conference (trap): Set about 35 days before trial before Judge Marbley. Trial counsel and parties or principals with settlement authority must attend; telephone availability requires a written motion for good cause at least 1 week ahead, and unexcused absence draws sanctions. Plaintiff serves a fully documented written demand 14 days before the conference and each opponent responds in writing 10 days before. Each party sends chambers only a letter of no more than 3 pages (theory of the case, settlement position in monetary terms, all conditions) 7 days before. Counsel must discuss with clients whether a summary jury trial or other ADR is appropriate; the judge encourages summary jury trials.

docs.x: Judge Algenon L. Marbley, S.D. Ohio. docs.t: Judge Algenon L. Marbley (S.D. Ohio) — Courtroom conduct
docs.x: Judge Algenon L. Marbley, S.D. Ohio. Courtroom conduct: Voir dire, openings, closings, and all addresses to the court are from the lectern; stand to address the court. Cross-examination is from the lectern; on direct counsel may move in the well. Ask permission to approach a witness or confer with co-counsel; one attorney per witness. Object standing, to the court only, stating just the grounds; argument only with permission. No colloquy between counsel, no first names, and no addressing jurors individually. Mobile devices, including texting and emailing, are strictly prohibited during status conferences.

docs.t: Judge Algenon L. Marbley (S.D. Ohio) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Algenon L. Marbley, S.D. Ohio. Jury selection: Civil juries have 8 members; the verdict must be unanimous and no verdict will be taken from fewer than 6 unless the parties stipulate. Each civil party has 3 peremptory challenges, exercised alternately, plaintiff first, against jurors in the box; a pass counts as used. The whole panel is examined in one continuous examination; the court conducts preliminary voir dire, and counsel may supplement without repeating questions, addressing the whole panel. Background questions are covered by the juror questionnaires, which counsel should review. In criminal cases, peremptories follow a fixed sequence (government 6, defendant 10, defendant taking two at a time early), then alternates in the same manner.

docs.x: Judge Herman Jacob Weber, S.D. Ohio. docs.t: Judge Timothy Black (S.D. Ohio) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Timothy Black, S.D. Ohio. docs.x: Judge Timothy Black, S.D. Ohio. docs.t: Judge Timothy Black (S.D. Ohio) — Summary judgment (trap)

Nonconforming briefs may be struck, and a conforming brief must be refiled within 30 days to preserve the motion.

docs.t: Judge Timothy Black (S.D. Ohio) — Motions and briefs

docs.x: Judge Timothy Black, S.D. Ohio. Civil jury selection and trial: Eight jurors are seated and all deliberate. docs.t: Judge James L. Graham (S.D. Ohio) — RICO case statement: deadline and form (trap)
docs.x: Judge James L. Graham, S.D. Ohio. RICO case statement: deadline and form (trap): In any case with a civil RICO claim, the plaintiff must file a RICO case statement within 20 days of the standing order. It must state the facts the plaintiff relies on as a result of the Rule 11 “reasonable inquiry.” The statement must use the order’s numbers and letters and answer each of its 20 items in detail and with specificity.

docs.t: Judge James L. Graham (S.D. Ohio) — RICO statement: parties and predicate acts
docs.x: Judge James L. Graham, S.D. Ohio. RICO statement: parties and predicate acts: State which of § 1962(a), (b), (c), and/or (d) is allegedly violated; list each defendant with its alleged misconduct and basis of liability; list other alleged wrongdoers and their misconduct; and list the alleged victims and how each was injured. For each RICO claim, describe the pattern of racketeering or collection of unlawful debt: the predicate acts and statutes violated, their dates, participants, and facts, how they relate to each other, how they form a pattern, and how they amount to or threaten continuing racketeering activity. Predicate acts of wire fraud, mail fraud, or securities fraud must be pleaded with Rule 9(b) particularity: the time, place, and contents of the misrepresentations, and who made them to whom.

docs.t: Judge James L. Graham (S.D. Ohio) — RICO statement: the enterprise
docs.x: Judge James L. Graham, S.D. Ohio. RICO statement: the enterprise: For each RICO claim, name the individuals or entities that make up the enterprise; describe its structure, purpose, function, and course of conduct; and state whether each defendant is an employee, officer, or director of it, or associated with it. State whether defendants are separate from the enterprise, are the enterprise itself, or are members of it (and, if so, whether they are perpetrators, passive instruments, or victims), and whether the pattern and the enterprise are separate or have merged. Describe the relationship between the enterprise’s activities and the pattern, how the racketeering differs from its usual activities, any benefits it received, and its effect on interstate or foreign commerce.

docs.t: Judge James L. Graham (S.D. Ohio) — RICO statement: section-specific items
docs.x: Judge James L. Graham, S.D. Ohio. RICO statement: section-specific items: § 1962(a): who received the income from the racketeering or unlawful debt, and how it was used or invested. § 1962(b): the acquisition or maintenance of any interest in or control of the enterprise. § 1962(c): who was employed by or associated with the enterprise, and whether the same entity is both the liable “person” and the “enterprise.” § 1962(d): the alleged conspiracy, in detail.

docs.t: Judge James L. Graham (S.D. Ohio) — RICO statement: injury, damages, and other claims
docs.x: Judge James L. Graham, S.D. Ohio. RICO statement: injury, damages, and other claims: Describe the injury to business or property and the direct causal relationship between the injury and the RICO violation, and list the damages, with the amount for which each defendant is allegedly liable. List all other federal causes of action (with statute numbers) and all pendent state claims, and add any other information that would help the court process the RICO claim.
